title: Command success: $?, &&, || and error messages
lead: No output does not mean an error. Every command leaves an exit status; in this module you learn to read it, chain commands based on it and understand error messages.
objectives: You read the last command's exit status with `echo $?` and tell 0 from non-zero.
You chain commands conditionally with `true`, `false`, `&&`, `||` and `;`.
You know the difference between stdout and stderr and separate errors with `2>`.
You read `Permission denied`, `No such file or directory` and `command not found` and find the cause.
You test files, numbers and strings with `test` and `[ ]`.

sections.title: Exit status: $?
body: When a command finishes it produces an **exit status**. **0 = success**, any other number = failure. A silent command (such as `mkdir`) may have succeeded or failed; to be sure, type `echo $?`.
Common codes: `1` general error, `2` misuse or missing path (`ls`), `126` not executable, `127` command not found, `130` interrupted with Ctrl+C.
Careful: `$?` is overwritten after every command. An `echo $?` typed right afterwards leaves its own result (0); read the code **immediately after the command in question**.

commands.what: Prints the exit status of the last command.
commands.why: Shows with a number whether the command really worked.

commands.what: Does nothing and always ends with 0.
commands.where: Testing chains and loops when you need a 'successful' command.

commands.what: Does nothing and always ends with 1.

sections.tip: No output is not an error. Most Unix commands are silent on success.

sections.title: Chaining: &&, || and ;
body: `A && B`: B runs only if A **succeeded** (0). `A || B`: B runs only if A **failed**. `A ; B`: B runs in every case.
The classic pattern: `mkdir lab && cd lab` (enter the folder if it was created). `A && B || C` acts like an if/else, but if B fails C runs too, so use it only for simple cases.

commands.what: Runs the right side if the left side succeeded.
commands.where: Steps that depend on each other.
commands.why: Prevents carrying on after a failed step.

commands.what: Runs the right side if the left side failed.
Runs commands in order regardless of success.
commands.where: Writing independent commands on one line.
commands.why: Keeps the order, ignores the result.

sections.warn: In chains like `rm -r old_project ; ...` using `;` runs the destructive command even if the previous step failed. Join destructive steps with `&&`.

sections.title: stdout and stderr
body: Every command has two output channels: **stdout** (channel 1, normal output) and **stderr** (channel 2, error messages). Both appear on screen, but they can be redirected separately.

`>` sends only stdout to a file; the error stays on screen. `2>` sends errors to a file. `2>/dev/null` throws errors away. `2>&1` sends stderr to wherever stdout goes. Note: redirection **does not change the exit status**; even if the error is hidden, the command still failed.

commands.what: Writes error messages (stderr) to a file.

commands.why: Keeps output clean, but also hides real problems.

commands.what: Redirects stderr to the same place as stdout.
commands.where: Collecting output and errors in one file or pipeline.
commands.why: Keeps the complete record in one place.

sections.title: Reading error messages
body: An error message usually looks like `program: argument: reason`. The first word is the program that failed, the second the problem path, the last the reason.

**No such file or directory**: the path does not exist or has a typo; check where you are with `ls` and `pwd`. **Permission denied**: the path exists but you lack permission; look at `ls -l`. **command not found** (code 127): wrong command name or not installed; check with `type` / `which`. **Is a directory**: you gave a folder to a command that expects a file.

commands.where: Looking for the cause of Permission denied.
commands.why: You see which permission is missing.

commands.what: Tells you whether a name is a command, builtin or alias.

sections.danger: When you see Permission denied, do not reflexively type `sudo` or `chmod 777`. Understand the cause first; needlessly wide permissions are a security hole.

sections.title: Testing conditions: test and [ ]
body: `test` (and its equivalent `[ ... ]`) checks a condition and prints nothing; it reports the result only through its exit status: 0 if true, 1 if false. That is why it fits so well with `&&` / `||`.

Common ones: `-f` regular file, `-d` directory, `-e` exists, `-r`/`-w`/`-x` readable/writable/executable, `-z` string empty. For numbers `-eq -ne -gt -lt`, for strings `=` and `!=`. Inside `[ ]` the **spaces** next to the brackets are mandatory.

commands.what: Succeeds if the path exists and is a regular file.
commands.why: You avoid running a command on a missing file and getting an error.

commands.what: Succeeds if the path is a directory.
commands.where: E.g. creating a folder only if it is missing.

commands.why: Turns numeric conditions into an exit status.

sections.tip: Classic pattern: `test -d backup || mkdir backup`. It creates the folder if missing and leaves it alone otherwise.

t01.text: Run `pwd` first, then read its exit status right away with `echo $?`.
t01.hint: Type two separate lines; the code should be 0.

t02.text: List a path that does not exist: `ls /nonexistent`, and read the error message.
t02.hint: The error goes to stderr; it still shows on screen.

t03.text: Run `false`, then read its status with `echo $?`. What number do you get?

t04.text: In a single line write `mkdir lab && cd lab` to create the folder and enter it.
t04.hint: `&&` runs the second command only if the first succeeded.

t05.text: Type `cd /nonexistent || echo failed` and think about why `failed` is printed.
t05.hint: When `cd` fails, `||` runs the right-hand side.

t06.text: Predict: what does `cat missing.txt; echo $?` print and what is the code? Then run it to verify.
t06.hint: `cat` prints an error when it cannot find the file and exits with 1.

t07.text: Predict: what does `test -f notes.txt && echo yes || echo no` print? Run it to verify.
t07.hint: `notes.txt` exists in home and is a regular file.

t08.text: `cat locked.txt` gives 'Permission denied'. Understand why, fix it with `chmod` and read the file.
t08.hint: Give yourself read permission: `chmod u+r locked.txt`.

t09.text: `cp notes.txt backup/` fails because `backup` does not exist. Chain it: create the folder and copy the file.

t10.text: Mini project: (1) write the error of `ls /nonexistent` to `errors.txt`, (2) write the output of `ls ~` to `files.txt`, (3) read the last command's status with `echo $?`.
t10.hint: Use `2>` for the error and `>` for the output.

t11.text: Mini project: in one line create the `project` folder, enter it, create the file `main.txt` and finally print `built`.
t11.hint: Join four commands with `&&`; you can use `mkdir -p project`.

t12.text: Challenge: create the `backup` folder if it is missing; copy `notes.txt` into it; if the copy succeeded write `saved` into `status.txt`, otherwise `failed`.
t12.hint: `test -d backup || mkdir backup` and `cp ... && echo saved > status.txt || echo failed > status.txt`.

t13.text: Challenge: does `notes.txt` contain `hello`? Test it in one line and print `found` or `missing`; discard grep's own output to `/dev/null`.
t13.hint: `grep hello notes.txt > /dev/null && echo found || echo missing`.

t14.text: Ticket: A colleague says 'I cannot read my report' and tried `cat Documents/raport.txt`. Find the right name with `ls Documents`, read the file with `cat` and write the exit status to `exit.txt`.
t14.hint: The right name is `report.txt`. `cat Documents/report.txt; echo $? > exit.txt`.

vm.intro: Run the following commands on your own VM (Ubuntu/Rocky/Alma or WSL); we only use safe, read-only commands. Paste the output and check it.

v01.title: Success and failure codes
v01.text: Run one successful and one failing command and read the code after each. Paste the whole output.

blocks.expected:
bin  boot  dev  etc ...
0
ls: cannot access '/nonexistent': No such file or directory
2

differs: A failing `ls` gives 2 (GNU ls); other commands may give 1. That is fine, what matters is that it is not 0.
If the message is localised it may be in another language; the code is the same.

v02.title: command not found: 127
v02.text: Run a command that does not exist and read the exit status.
differs: Ubuntu sometimes suggests a package with 'Command not found'; the code is still 127.
If you type `echo $?` twice the second gives 0; read it only right after the first command.

v03.title: How && and || behave
v03.text: Try the chains and see which side runs.

blocks.cmd:
true && echo ok
false && echo never
false || echo fallback
true ; echo always

differs: If `never` appears you may have typed `;` instead of `&&`.
If nothing prints, look for a quote or spacing mistake.

v04.title: Permission denied
v04.text: Open a file you cannot read as a normal user and paste the error and status (read-only, nothing changes).
differs: If you are root the file opens; switch to a normal user (`su - student` or a new user).
On older systems you can try `/etc/sudoers` instead of `/etc/shadow`.

v05.title: Conditions with test
v05.text: Test file and directory conditions. Paste the result as `yes` / `no`.

blocks.cmd:
test -d /etc && echo yes || echo no
test -f /etc/nonexistent && echo yes || echo no

differs: If both print `yes` you may have typed `-e` instead of `-f`.
When you write `[ -d /etc ]`, do not forget the spaces around `[` and `]`.

q1.q: What is the exit status of a command that finished successfully?
q1.explain: 0 means success; every non-zero value indicates a failure.

q2.q: When does B run in the line `A && B`?
q2.explain: `&&` acts like AND; B runs only if A ends with 0.

q3.explain: 127 = command not found. A permission problem is 126, Ctrl+C is 130.

options: Shows the error message and prints 0
Hides the error message but the status stays non-zero
q4.explain: `2>/dev/null` only discards the message; the command still failed and `$?` is not 0.

summary: Exit status: 0 is success, anything else is an error. Read it immediately with `echo $?`.
`&&` continues on success, `||` on failure, `;` in every case.
stdout is redirected with `>`, stderr with `2>`; redirection does not change the exit status.
Error message: program, path, reason. 127 = no such command, Permission denied = no permission.
`test` and `[ ]` turn conditions into an exit status.

glossary.meaning: The number a command leaves when it finishes; 0 = success.
Operator that runs the right side if the left side succeeded.
Operator that runs the right side if the left side failed.
